newsitem.title: USA: U.S. FTC says Exxon used misleading ads.
newsitem.headline: U.S. FTC says Exxon used misleading ads.

text.p: The U.S. Federal Trade Commission Tuesday charged that Exxon Corporation has misled consumers by making unsubstantiated advertising claims for its gasoline.
While the FTC said the ads allegedly claim that switching to Exxon 93 Supreme will make engines cleaner and cut car maintenance costs, it said Exxon failed to substantiate these claims.
If is charges are upheld in a trial with an administrative law judge, Exxon would have to produce scientific support for future claims of its fuel's benefits, the FTC said.

"In this case, consumers may be paying as much as twenty cents a gallon more for premium gasoline, because of claims that it will make engines cleaner and cheaper to maintain," Jodie Bernstein, director of the FTC Bureau of Consumer Protection, said in a statement.
The FTC said this case was the latest in a series of cases challenging deceptive ads claims for high octane fuel.
It said Amoco Oil Corp, Sun Company and Unocal Corp have settled FTC charges in connection with superiority claims for their high octane gasolines.
Exxon, the largest oil company in the United States, does business in more than 100 countries and had revenues of $124 billion in 1995, the FTC said.
According to the FTC complaint, Exxon aired television and radio ads that included statements such as "Exxon gasoline keeps your engine cleaner...So it can help you drive down maintenance costs."

Under the order the FTC is seeking, Exxon would have to have scientific substantiations for such claims and any other engine performance, power, acceleration, or cleaning claims it makes for gasoline in the future.
A comment from Exxon was not immediately available.

"Federal regulations require that all gasolines at all octane levels contain sufficient detergent additives to keep engines clean. In these times of high gasoline prices, spending more money for high octane fuel that your car doesn't need is just a way of picking your own pocket," Bernstein of the FTC said in a statement.
